column2: the writer's notes (doubts; where the article disagrees with the entry): for the data check
The article dates the grant of the style His Highness to 30 February 1819, an impossible date; the day is left out.

The article dates the construction of the Temple of the Obelisks to around 1600 BCE, while the entry dates it to the early 2nd millennium BCE (and the Abishemu obelisk found in it is c. 1800 BCE). The construction date is left out.

The article gives the Late Postclassic occupation as c. 1200-1519 CE (and an Epiclassic phase 600-900 CE), while the entry says Tepeticpac was founded in the 14th century; the phase dates are left out. The article itself says the founding chronology is debated. The article says INAH works began in 2009 and also that the project started in 2010, and that the site museum was to open in 2025 but that work began in early 2026; these dates are left out.
The article gives his death as 1526 in its lead but as February 1527 in the text (and his reign as 1482-1527); the year of death is left out.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words and adds little beyond the description
The quoted advertisement for the music prize gives the closing date as 30 October 1850, evidently a slip for 1859; not used.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance; it adds only the army, the tribute figures and the family

Left out as doubtful or hyperbolic in the article: that he was the first in New England to free his slaves (1646), that he served as ambassador between James I and Christian IV, and the claim that he is the Father of American Law (the article itself calls this hyperbole). The article's account of the move to New Haven is confused (the site named New Haven on 14 April 1638, then an exploration that autumn finding Quinnipiack); only the November agreement is used.
The article dates his death to May 1542 (born 1505, king 1527-1542) and the defeat outside Prome to April 1542, while the entry gives 1543. The years of the defeat and the death are left out.

The article says he 'became an active Orangeman' but later that 'there is no evidence that he ever claimed the Orange Order'; the entry says he was a member. Neither point is repeated here. The article gives his birth as 1 January 1842; the entry has c. 1842, so only the year is given.

The article defines the historic territory as Quang Tri, Hue (Thua Thien), Da Nang and northern Quang Nam, while the entry says roughly Quang Tri and Thua Thien Hue; the modern extent is left out. The article gives no year for Nguyen Hoang's appointment (the entry says 1558).

SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance; beyond the description it gives only the verse structure, the 2012 prefectural designation and two later uses (Sakamoto's Beauty, the film Japanese Story)
The article dates the division of Ailech into Tír Eoghain and Tír Conaill both to the 12th century and to the 13th century; the century is left out.

The article says the da Costa family descended from Portuguese Jewish merchants and the Hornay were Dutch; the entry calls the community of mixed Portuguese, Indian and Southeast Asian descent. Left the family origins out. The article says warfare between the two Portuguese groups lasted for long periods up to 1785; left out.

The article's lead gives his death as 31 December 1830 (as the entry's dates), but its text says he died in Murcia on 1 January 1829, aged seventy-nine, and is muddled about whether he went to Madrid. Left the death out.

The article dates a Tamil seminary to 1707 in one place and a seminary for native clergy to 1716 in another; left the date out. It also says Ziegenbalg translated the Bible in 1715, but elsewhere that at his death in 1719 he had finished only the New Testament and Genesis to Ruth; used the second.
SKIPPED: article has about 250 words of substance, most of it already in the entry; not enough for 260 words without padding
Short article (about 270 words); all of it is used here.
SKIPPED: article is under 300 words, almost all a list of the territories exchanged; too little to add to the entry without padding
Short article (about 300 words); all its substance is used here.
The article names the governor only as Seymour.
SKIPPED: article is under 300 words and the entry already gives most of it (size, altar); too little for a longer text
The article gives the state constitution's clause on their election as Pt.1 Ch.3 in one place and Pt.1 Ch.5 in another; left clause numbers out.
The article says he was elected Dey in 1593 and took real power in 1598; the entry has him dey from 1598. Wrote that the militia elected him its head in the 1590s, without the year or the title.

The article dates the founding of the capital and Vanraj's accession variously (746 or 765, Merutuṇga giving both) and his reign as c. 746 to c. 780; the entry says the city was founded around 746. Left all dates of his reign and the city out. In Merutuṇga's story a nun named Vīramatī brought up the boy and he was returned to his mother; the entry says he was raised by a Jain monk. Wrote only of the monk's part.
The article gives the new consensus for his reign as c. 85-125 CE (earlier 110-138 or 130-159 CE); the entry places him in the second century CE. Left all reign dates out.
SKIPPED: article too thin: about 250 words, most of it already in the description The article dates his accession to 1634; the entry says r. 1633.

The article's lead dates his governorship of Lagos 1904 to 1906, but its body says he became governor in 1903; the entry says 1904. The year he took office is left out. The article's career dates in Malaya are not in a consistent order (acting Resident at Penang in 1894 is placed before First Magistrate in 1888); only the posts are given.
The article dates Henry the Fowler's stay at Werla to 924 or 926, depending on how the evidence is read; the entry says 926. No year is given in the text.

The article says the agency was merged with the Baroda and Gujarat States Agency on 5 November 1944 to form the Baroda, Western India and Gujarat States Agency; the entry's dates run to 1947. The 1944 merger is left out of the text. The 1941 population is given in the article in Indian notation as 52,20,011; the text says just over five million.

The article says the commission was established in 1758 by the Parliament Street Act 1757; the entry dates it 1757. The text gives no year of foundation. The article dates the widening of Essex Bridge to 1755, before the commission existed; the year is left out.
The article does not mention Dushak or the Baku commissars, which the entry names; nothing is added on them.
The article says Worcester and eleven other missionaries signed the protest, then that all eleven men were convicted, of whom nine accepted pardons; the count is left out.

The article calls him the grandson of Gazi Gümüshtigin and son of Emir Gazi, and the uncle of Melik Zünnun; the entry calls him a son of Gümüştekin Gazi. His parentage, and his relation to Zinnun, are left out of the text. The article gives no start date for his rule; the entry says about 1142.
SKIPPED: article too thin: under 250 words of substance (an empty coinage section, two inscriptions and the Matsya Purana's 29 years)

The article dates his reign c. 925–953; the entry says c. 925–950. The end of the reign is not given. The entry says he took Kalinjar from the Gurjara-Pratiharas; the article says the enemy in this campaign is uncertain (the Pratiharas, or the Rashtrakutas who may have taken it from them). The text names no enemy. The Khajuraho inscription is dated 953-954 CE in the article; the date is left out because it falls after the entry's end of reign.

The article says Liu Rengong himself declared himself King of Yan; the entry speaks of his son's short-lived Yan state. Who took the title is left out. The article does not name An Lushan, whom the entry names; it mentions only the Anshi Rebellion.
The article gives his death as 28 April 1912; the entry's dates end in 1909. His death is left out.

The article dates his first reign 1578 to 1579 and his accession to 1578 (his father died in December 1578); the entry says he reigned in 1579. The year of accession is left out. The article says he died at Puri in Orissa and was buried at Biswak in Bihar; the entry says he died in exile in Bihar. The place of death is left out; only the burial is given. The article does not name Habba Khatun; it mentions only his separation from the love of his life.
The article calls the town both Cap-Haïtien and Cap-Francais; the entry's Cap-Haïtien is used.

Rumphius (1678) put his death around 1510, against the entry's d. c. 1500; left out. The article lists the Hikayat's version that he died at sea on the return voyage and Valentijn's that he reached Ternate; both told as accounts, as the entry says only that he is credited with the change. The oldest chronicle, the Hikayat Tanah Hitu, says he himself first converted; Valentijn says his father Marhum was the first convert. Not resolved in the text.

The article says Laihur received the title of khan at the beginning of the 17th century, yet was murdered in 1587, while its list gives Laihur (?-1596); the entry says the title was adopted in the late 16th century. The dates of Laihur's title and death are left out. The article speaks of four Khalkha khanates from the start; the entry says three, later four. No count given in the text. The article spells Dayan Khan's son Gersenji; the son is left unnamed in the text so as not to depart from the entry's spelling Geresenje.

The article gives his death as 28 January 919 (the battle fell in the Chinese year of 918); the entry gives d. 918. No exact date of death given in the text. The capital, the entry's Youzhou (the article's You Prefecture), is left unnamed in the text.

The article dates Liu Yu's decision and Zhu's appointment against Qiao Zong to 413; the entry says Liu Yu gave him command in 412. No year given for the appointment in the text. The article calls the state Qiao Shu; the entry's name Western Shu kept by not naming the state.

The article says Zibhebhu vied for the royal succession with another of Cetshwayo's sons, which would make him Cetshwayo's son and conflicts with its own genealogy; left out. The article does not tell his later life or his death in 1904, so there is no death section.

The article's full name is the Judicial Commission of Inquiry into Allegations of State Capture, Corruption and Fraud in the Public Sector including Organs of State; the entry gives the shorter form, so no formal name repeated here. Testimony is attributed to the witnesses and findings to the commission; living people named only as the commission and witnesses named them.

The article dates him fl. c. 2370 BC, which is the 24th century BCE; the entry dates him to the 23rd century BCE. No date given in the text. The article places Marhashi only somewhere on the Iranian plateau; the entry's location east of Elam is not repeated.

The article dates his submission to Menelik to 1884; the entry says 1882. No year given for the submission in the text. The article says he incorporated the conquered part of Janjero into his own kingdom; the entry says he helped bring Janjero under Ethiopian rule. The text says only that he conquered part of it. The article spells the capital Jeren; the entry's Jiren is not contradicted, as the text does not name it.

The article dates his proclamation as caliph to 765, after the death of Khaled ibn Hamid; the entry says he was proclaimed imam at Tlemcen around 742. No date given in the text. The article says he founded Agadir (Tlemcen) in 790 on the ruins of Roman Pomaria, and elsewhere that he was its founder during his reign of 776-778; both conflict with the entry, which has him proclaimed at Tlemcen around 742. Left out. The article spells the town of the entry's siege Tobna; the town is not named in the text, to keep the entry's spelling Tubna unchallenged.

The article also counts him as shehu of the Kanem-Bornu Empire under French protection in 1900 and 1901-1902, before the British appointment; the entry dates his rule from 1902. The earlier period is told as background, without calling it his reign. The incumbent shehu, Garbai's grandson, is living and is left out.

The article says roughly half of the affranchis were free people of colour and 'the other half African slaves'; read as Africans who had been enslaved and freed. The article uses 'mulattoes'; rendered as men of mixed descent.
The entry says the revolt was crushed and Agüeybaná II was killed; the article says it is presumed the warrior shot before the battle was he. Kept with the article's hedge.

The article spells the designer Ram Singh Malam; the designer is left unnamed in the text, as the entry names him Ramsinh Malam. The article's claim that the horoscope is believed to be the longest in the world is left out.

The article dates his election to 749 and his death to 751, with the imamate conquered by 752; the entry has him elected around 750 and killed in 752. No year given for the election or the death in the text.

The article calls him 19 when he moved to Jesselton on 15 May 1941, which does not fit a birth in 1921; his age left out. Another source in the article says he learned his medical skills in Penang; left out.

The article says the present church was begun in the late 8th or early 9th century, by King Offa of Mercia or his successor Coenwulf; the entry dates it probably to the late 7th or 8th century. No date or builder given for the church in the text.
The entry says Alsium was a harbour of Caere; the article does not mention Caere, so nothing is added on that.

The article says Amadu II was killed in 1852 and Seku Amadu died in 1844; the entries give 1853 and 1845 (Amadu II's own article also gives 1845 and February 1853). Those years left out. The article spells the capital Hamdallahi and Hamdullahi; the entry's Hamdullahi used. The Kunta leader is spelt both al-Bakkay and al-Bekkay in the article.
The article spells the capital Hamdallahi; the entry's Hamdullahi used. The article's statement that the empire stretched from just downstream of Segu is rendered 'just below Segu'.

The article spells the royal seat Niki-Niki; the entry's Niki Niki used. The article's statement on the present religion of the population (mostly Protestant) left out as a present-day detail not needed.

The article gives his death as February 1781 at the age of 34; the entry dates him 1748–1782 and his rule to 1782. The death year and age are left out. The article names the Afghan ruler Ahmed Shah Abdali; the entry's form Ahmad Shah Durrani is used.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance; beyond the entry it adds only two court plots and his unfinished tomb
The article dates his birth c. 1772 and says most estimates place it between 1770 and 1790; the entry has c. 1789. The birth year is left out.

The entry says the agreement blocked German plans for a railway terminus; the article names only the Russian Vladimir Kapnist's railway plan as what brought Britain back to negotiations. Both are kept as they stand (no direct contradiction), but the editor may wish to check the entry's German railway point.

The article gives two versions of his death: in 1852 after suppressing a rebellion at Camargo, or at his house in Miquihuana, Tamaulipas, on 19 January 1869. The entry dates him 1802–1852; his death is left out.
SKIPPED: article is thin (his parentage, upbringing and marriage only, then a book list) and says nothing of his reign beyond the entry; it also dates his rule 1583-1586

The article dates his reign 1529–1531 and his proclamation at Gao to 15 August 1529; the entry has 1528–1531. The year of his proclamation is left out (Ali Fulan's exile in 1528 is kept, as it does not date the accession). The article spells his father Askia Mohammad; the entry's Askia Muhammad is used.

The article dates his reign 18 November 1722 – 21 May 1755 and his death to 21 May 1755; the entry has d. 1756. The year of his death is left out. The article calls Jai Singh II 'of Jaipur'; the entry 'Sawai Jai Singh II of Amber'. Written 'Jai Singh II of Jaipur' once.

Left out the article's population figures (over 10 million for Bakil, 4 million for Hashid) and its naming of current leaders. The article dates Khalid ibn al-Walid's mission to Yemen to 622 and writes 'By the 10th century ... in 893-7'; the year 622 is left out and al-Hadi's arrival given as the end of the 9th century.
The article's local descriptions (fishing enclosures, aloe trade, fairs) read like an old gazetteer; they are given in the past tense or as customs, without dating them.
The article's title spells the work Parhaego; the entry's spelling Balhaego is used. The article gives no date of completion (the entry has 1784).

The article gives his reign as 1160–1178; the entry has d. c. 1179. These do not contradict each other (he retired before he died), so neither date is used. The article's statement that the Kulin classification has 'no historical authenticity' is kept as the article puts it; the entry says tradition credits him with it.
The article spells the painter Nihâl Chand; the entry's Nihal Chand is used.

The entry says British and French forces defeated Niumi; the article mentions no French forces (only the French post at Albreda as a trade rival). The text names only the British forces the article names and does not mention the French either way. The article does not give the treaty's terms; the entry's statement that Niumi confirmed the cession of the Ceded Mile is not repeated.
The article says the chiefs convinced Queen Victoria; the entry says the Colonial Office. The text says only that they won the guarantee.

The entry says Duke Qing escaped when his charioteer changed places with him; the article says he switched places with Feng Choufu, his chariot's spearman, while Bing Xia was his driver. The text names Feng Choufu without his role; the editor may wish to correct the entry's 'charioteer'. The Guliang Zhuan's version of the insult (each envoy given a servant with his own physical defect) is left out for length.

The article calls the Ghurid sultan Muhammad of Ghor and the Khwarazmshah Alauddin Shah; the entry names them Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad and Muhammad II. The article's names are kept for checking; the editor may change them to the entry's. The article gives Tayangu's home as both Taraz (lead) and Talas (body).

The article dates the battle 18 September 1686 or 1688; the entry gives 1688. No date is given in the text. The entry names Fateh Shah of Garhwal and his allies as the Guru's opponents; the article treats Bhim Chand of Bilaspur as the leader of the alliance with Fateh Shah and 14 other rajas. The text names both as allies without saying who led. The article contradicts itself on who killed Hayat Khan (Mahant Kirpal Das, or the Guru's maternal uncle Kirpal Chand); left out. Also left out the Guru's age at the battle (19), which depends on the disputed year.

The article gives different days: the Nawanagar office notes (Shraavana Vad 7, VS 1648, July 1591), the Akbarnama (14-18 July 1591) and the Tarikh-i-Sorath (a later Hindu and Hijri date). The text only says the sources differ. Casualty totals left out: the article says both armies lost more than 10,000, but also that 2,000 Kathiawar soldiers and 100-200 Mughal soldiers died.

The article dates the battle to August 1261 in its lead and to July 1261 in its causes section; no month is given in the text. The article's lead mentions three Irish clans but names only the MacCarthys; the others are not named in the text.

The king is not named in the text: the entry spells him Cunipert, the article Cunicpert and Cunincpert. The article calls Alahis duke of Trent only; the entry's 'Trent and Brescia' is not repeated or contradicted.
The article calls the conflict the North-West Rebellion (and Northwest Resistance in a quotation); the entry says North-West Resistance. The text names neither.

Maba's brother appears in the article as both Abdoulaye Oulimata Ba and Abdoulaye Ouli Ba; the text uses the second. The article says that according to some, Makhoureja Ngoneh Joof was responsible for killing Maba; left out as uncertain.
SKIPPED: the article has under 250 words of substance and adds only Ken Arok's rise to the entry's description; it dates the battle to 1221 or 1222 (the entry: 1222)

SKIPPED: the article says the battle may never have happened: its only detailed account is E. A. Ritter's Shaka Zulu (1955), and the historian Dan Wylie concludes Ritter fabricated it from a passing mention in Bryant's Olden Times; it appears in no Zulu oral tradition. The entry states the battle and its losses as fact and needs review; a longer text would contradict it. The article: 'claimed by some to have occurred on or around April 1818'; Wylie, History in Africa 1992 and 1993. The two possible references to the hill (Kwa Qori) are both defeats for Shaka.

The prince and the khan are not named in the text: the entry spells them Kurgoko Atazhukin and Kaplan I Giray, the article Kurghoqo Hatokhshoqo and Qaplan I Giray. The entry says the army was 'sent by' the khan; the article has the khan leading it in person. The text says the khan camped and fled, which the entry does not exclude. The article places the battle near the village of Bylym on the Baksan River in its lead but has the khan's camp on the upper Malka; the village is left out. Casualty figures in the sources vary widely (over 30,000, 11,000, more than 5,000); only the commander's figure is given, attributed.

The article disagrees with the entry on the main point. It dates the battle July 1391 or 1392 (Zachariadou argues for 1391; the entry says 1392), names the Ottoman commander as Ertugrul Celebi, son of Bayezid, and says Manuel II's letters show no major clash and an Ottoman success overall, Zachariadou holding that the Ottomans merely withdrew after a raid. The text gives the battle only as Ibn Ardashir tells it, attributed, and leaves out the year, the commander and Manuel's contrary reading of the outcome. The entry may need revising.

SKIPPED: the article has under 250 words; beyond the entry it adds only the Holkar leaders' ages, Roshan Beg's 63 guns and the desertion of Gafur Khan The article names only Sir Thomas Hislop as British commander; the entry adds Sir John Malcolm.

The entry says Tany crossed in breach of a truce; the article does not mention a truce. Not repeated. The article says the conquest was completed within two months of the battle; the entry says 1283. The text gives no time.

The high king is named only as Domnall: the entry calls him Domnall mac Aedo, the article Domnall II. The article calls Congal King of Ulaid and says he first established his power base in Dal Riata, where he became king; the entry calls him king of the Dal nAraidi. The Dal Riata kingship is left out. The article says the site is not settled and some place it outside Newry (Sheeptown, Derrylecklagh, the Crown Mound); the entry places it near Moira. Left out.

The article has the column camp on the night of the 20th and fight 'the next day', which would be 21 January; the entry dates the battle 22 January 1824. No day is given in the text. The entry says MacCarthy 'was killed'; the article says he was wounded and killed himself rather than be taken prisoner. The text follows the article, which the entry's wording does not exclude; the editor may want to check.

The ruler of Samarkand is not named: the entry spells him Yalangtush Bahadur, the article Yalangto'sh Bakhodir. The article's figures (outnumbered 1:25; the Dzungars 'lost from eleven thousand men') are garbled in places; the ratio is left out and the losses hedged. The last paragraph is about 40 words; the article says little more of the aftermath.
The article's chronology of the Puerto Rican aid is confused (a ship reaching Puerto Rico on 28 November with news that aid would come); left out.
SKIPPED: the article has about 250 words and adds almost nothing to the entry beyond troop numbers (Xue Ju's 300,000, Zong Luohou's 100,000) and a stalemate of about 60 days

The article places the battlefield both 350 km and 140 km from Aurangabad; no distance given. The article says the post Nizam-ul-Mulk regained in 1725 was one he had held 1721-1723, but also that he was prime minister in Delhi from 1721; those years left out. The article's 'title of Asaf Jahi dynasty' is garbled; written as honours conferred, with the dynasty named. Bajirao's reward is given as '7,000 Mansabdars and 7,000 horses', which reads like a mansab rank; the figure left out. The article twice says no source verifies Mubariz Khan's death; the entry states it, so the text keeps the death and says the details are thinly attested.

The article dates the battle to 968 throughout (Brian's band 'by the year 968', 'summer of 968'), while the annal entries it quotes are numbered AI967.2 and U967.5 and the entry says 967. No year given in the text. The article has the fighting last 'from dawn until dusk', 'from dusk until dawn' and also says the Norse fled 'by mid-day': duration left out. Left out the article's dubious details: Brian's birth in 942, his father killed in a Viking raid, and 'Brian's journal'. The article names Brian as leader; the entry names Mathgamain and Brian. The text names both as the annals and the Cogad do.
The article's spelling 'Mohamud Shah' in one place is a slip for Mahmud Shah. Short article; three sections kept, the second brief.
The article gives 1 April 1825 in its lead and 2 April 1825 in its body; the entry says 1 April. No day given in the text.

SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance; beyond the description it adds only the author's stay at the Jalayirid court and a short passage on his choice of Persian The article translates the title 'Banquets and Battles'; the entry has 'Feast and Battle'.

The article dates the cross 'probably 7th or early 8th century' in its lead and reports a theory (Meyer Schapiro, the Bewcastle website) that Benedict Biscop's masons of the 670s made it; the entry says 'probably early eighth century'. The text gives only the consensus for the first half of the eighth century. The article does not say which face carries the sundial; left unnamed. The 2007 scholar is left unnamed: the article spells him 'Ó Carragaáin', a slip for Ó Carragáin. The article's line 'Alfredir was king of Northumbria, and died around 664' is garbled; left out.

The entry places the community in western Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat and Maharashtra; the article says they are recognised as Scheduled Tribes in Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan. The states are not named in the text. The article's population of 'around 150,000' sits beside the 1911 census and the Bhopawar Agency, but the article gives it no date; written as an estimate of the past. The article's remark that the elite chiefs 'paradoxically' claim pure Rajput descent without evidence is left out as a judgement.

The article says he was promoted to Major 'by 1948', but its own list of titles gives Major in 1944 and Brigadier from 1948; ranks left out. The article gives his wife's birth as 1 April 1916, which would make her 14 at the marriage of 1930; her birth date left out. The article calls him 'Maharaja' and says he ruled 1940-1947; the entry calls him Maharao. The text avoids the title in the heading sentence.

The article spells the state Kurwai in one list and Korwai in another, and Narsingarh and Narsinghgarh; the entry's spellings Kurwai and Narsinghgarh are used throughout. The article does not name Sehore, which the entry gives as the political agent's seat.

The article dates his death to 29 December 1550 ('some sources suggest 1551') and his reign to 1521-1550; the entry has d. 1551 and 1521-1551. No year of death given in the text. The article calls the father both Vijayabahu VI and 'Vijaya Bahu VII'; the entry's Vijayabahu VI is used. The article does not mention the embassy to Lisbon or Kelaniya as the place of death, both in the entry.

The entry names American Factors among the five; the article names H. Hackfeld & Co. (later Amfac) and does not mention American Factors. The text uses Hackfeld and Amfac only. The entry puts their dominance in the late 19th and early 20th centuries and their decline after the Second World War; the article dates the decline to the 1954 Democratic Revolution and statehood in 1959. The text keeps the article's dates, which fit within the entry's wording. Left out: Alexander & Baldwin's rank among landowners and the 2012 sale of Lanai (present-day business detail).

SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance and adds little to the description (the 1865 sénatus-consulte, the groups to be enfranchised first, the Crémieux Decree) The entry calls Viollette a former governor-general of Algeria; the article says he acted as governor-general. The article also names Messali Hadj's Étoile Nord-Africaine among the protesters, where the entry speaks only of settler opposition.

The article dates the work broadly between the sixth and tenth centuries (final form between 526 and 932), most likely near the earlier date; the entry says 6th century. The text gives the earlier limit and the likelihood, not the broad range. The article does not give the year of Moberg's edition (1924 in the entry).

The article dates his death to between 3 and 23 November 1591 and notes another source giving April 1591; the entry says 1591. The text follows the article's main account (November). The article's spelling Bréifne is replaced by the entry's West Breifne. The text says he was knighted around the parliament of 1585; the article says only that he was knighted in 1585 and attended the parliament that year.

The entry says the land was sold under 'the disputed treaties of 1838 and 1842'; the article says the agents worked 'beginning in 1837' without dating the first treaty. The text gives 'from 1837' for the agents' work and dates only the 1842 treaty. History paragraphs may be long; trimmed if flagged.

The entry places Bunkeya in Haut-Katanga province; the article says Lualaba Province. No province named in the text. The entry says Msiri was killed at Bunkeya in December 1891; the article says he fled to a nearby village where Omer Bodson killed him, and gives no date. The text names neither place nor month. The article's judgement that Msiri's rule 'had become tyrannical' is left out.

SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance; beyond the description it adds only a short summary of the stanzas and the song's later borrowings (Guillaume de Dole, Le roman de la violette, Dante, Ezra Pound)

The entry calls the poems the main source for the kingdom of Pengwern; the article speaks of Cynddylan as prince of Powys with his hall at Pengwern. The text follows Bray's summary as the article quotes it. The article mentions that some commentators consider a tenth-century date; the entry's 9th or 10th century covers this.

The article dates the first version to 1861-1862 and the Yale road to 1865; the entry's 1860-1865 is the span of construction. The article gives no total length (the entry has about 600 km). The camels and the mile houses belong to the 'Old Cariboo Road' from Lillooet, which the article treats as an informal use of the name; the text ties them to the Lillooet route.

The article dates the start of the narrative to the early Galuh period in the early 8th century; the entry says 'from the 7th century'. Left the century out. Poerbatjaraka's date is garbled in the article ('/91919-21)'); left out.
Short article; three sections kept brief. Left out the businesses (cannabis dispensaries, gaming) as present-day detail.

The article calls the post 'Viceroy of Yunnan and Guizhou'; the entry says governor-general, used here (same office). The entry dates the siege and capture of Dali 1872-1873; the article gives the capture in 1873. Not restated.
